checkpoints: Root cause 1: the `{cluster="prod"}` stream selector is too broad — it matches every stream/service in the prod cluster, forcing Loki to content-scan logs from all services before the regex ever runs.

The word "payments" inside the regex is doing work that the `job` label should be doing instead — label filtering happens via the index (cheap/instant), while matching "payments" in the regex requires scanning log content.

Fix for root cause 1: narrow the stream selector to `{cluster="prod", job="payments"}` so filtering happens via the index first, and drop the now-redundant "payments" substring from the regex since the label already scopes the content-scan to just payments logs before the regex runs.

Root cause 2: the regex `.*payments.*(timeout|time out|timed out).*` has redundant `.*` wrapped at both the start and end — LogQL line filters already do substring matching within a line, so no leading/trailing `.*` is needed, and keeping it forces unnecessary backtracking over the full line length.
Rewritten query: `{cluster="prod", job="payments"} |~ "(?i)(timeout|time out|timed out)"` — combining both fixes into a lean, index-first query with no redundant regex content.

Optional further optimization: if the three timeout phrases almost always appear exactly, replace `|~` with multiple `|=` substring filters joined by `or` for the common cases, keeping `|~` only for rarer variants.

Verify by comparing both elapsed query time (expecting a drop from ~40s to a few seconds) and result line count over the same test time range before/after the change, to confirm the query is faster while losing no real timeout logs.
A span is a TIMED unit of work (e.g. an HTTP handler, a DB query, or a call to another service), carrying a name plus a start and end timestamp used to compute duration.
Each span also carries a set of attributes (arbitrary key-value context, e.g. http.method=GET, db.statement=...) and a status (success or error, with an exception if applicable).

Each span carries three identifying fields: trace_id (the same across every span belonging to the same request, regardless of which service the span is in), span_id (unique to that specific span, never colliding with any other span), and parent_span_id (points back to the span_id of the span that called it, the parent).

As a request travels across services, each service creates a new span for its own work: it reads the shared trace_id from the received context, generates its own new span_id, and sets parent_span_id to exactly the span_id of the caller's span.
The tracing backend (Tempo, Jaeger) receives spans as discrete records arriving separately from different services, and uses trace_id to group all spans belonging to the same request together.
The tracing backend then uses the parent_span_id chain to arrange the grouped spans into a tree (not a flat list), reflecting correct nested/parallel/sequential call order.
A span with no parent_span_id (or an empty parent) is the root span, usually where the request first enters the system (e.g. at gateway).

Root cause: HTTP auto-instrumentation automatically injects trace context into the outbound request header and extracts it from the inbound request/response, so context flows through HTTP calls (gateway → orders) without any extra code.

An async boundary through a message queue like Kafka has no equivalent auto-instrumentation by default: when orders publishes a message, it doesn't automatically stuff trace context anywhere — a Kafka message is just a plain payload carrying no trace_id/span_id.

Consequence: the consumer has no context to read/attach to when it receives the message, so the OTel SDK creates a new root span with an entirely new trace_id unrelated to the original — this is why the consumer's work shows up as a separate, disconnected trace.

Fix on the publisher side: orders must actively inject the current trace context (from the active span) into a field in the Kafka message header before sending, using the SDK's inject() API right before producer.send().
Fix on the consumer side (extract): the consumer must actively extract the propagated context from the message header using the extract() API right when it receives the message.

Fix on the consumer side (attach as parent): the consumer must use the extracted context as the parent when creating the new processing span, so that parent_span_id correctly points to the publishing span and trace_id matches the original.

Verify by sending a test request across all 4 hops (gateway → orders → Kafka publish → consumer) and checking that all four pieces of work sit within one single trace tree; if two separate traces still appear, the inject or extract step is missing on one side.
Root cause: `RawHttpConnection` is a self-written/unfamiliar HTTP client that is not on the list of popular libraries the OTel auto-instrumentation agent already knows how to "wrap."

Auto-instrumentation works by patching/wrapping specific functions of known HTTP libraries (e.g. `requests`, `httpx`, `urllib3`) to automatically insert a `traceparent` header injection step every time that function is called — it is not a general mechanism that observes every byte leaving the process.

Because `RawHttpConnection` sits outside that list, no injection step happens, so the outgoing request carries no `traceparent`, and `inventory` sees no context to attach to — the same mechanism that breaks traces at a Kafka boundary, just with an un-instrumented HTTP client as the break point instead of a message queue.

Fix — setup: inside `call_inventory`, before sending the request, retrieve the current context (the active span already created by auto-instrumentation at `orders`'s request-handling framework layer).

Fix — inject: use a standard propagator (e.g. `TraceContextTextMapPropagator().inject(carrier)`) to build a carrier containing a properly W3C-formatted `traceparent` header, then manually attach that header to the request before calling `conn.request(...)`.

After the fix, the request sent from `orders` to `inventory` carries the correct `traceparent`, so `inventory`'s auto-instrumentation automatically reads the header and creates a child span with the correct `parent_span_id`.

Verify by sending a test request through `call_inventory` and checking that the trace now shows the `inventory` span correctly nested within the original request's trace tree — same `trace_id`, `parent_span_id` pointing to the span that called it in `orders` — no longer a separate trace.
Head-based sampling makes the keep/drop decision at the very start of the request, at the root span.
Head-based sampling makes its decision before the outcome (error or latency) of the request is known.
Head-based sampling applies a fixed, uniform probability roll to every request regardless of what that request turns out to be.
Head-based sampling is cheap and simple to implement because each service decides independently with no shared state across the system.

Because the head-based decision is outcome-blind, a rare error or an abnormally slow request is dropped at the same rate as an ordinary fast, successful request (e.g. 99% dropped at a 1% sample rate).
For a bug occurring in only 0.1% of requests, a 1% head-based sample keeps any given occurrence with probability only 1% x 0.1%, so that bug's trace is practically never captured.
Tail-based sampling makes the keep/drop decision only after the trace has fully completed, once every involved service has sent its spans.

Tail-based sampling can apply a smart policy because the full outcome is already known at decision time: keep 100% of error traces and slow traces (over a latency threshold), and aggressively down-sample only the fast, successful ones.
Tail-based sampling requires a stateful collector that holds all of a trace's spans in memory until that trace finishes before it can decide keep/drop, which carries a significant RAM cost.
Tail-based sampling adds operational complexity because every span belonging to the same trace must be routed to the same collector instance so it can see the whole trace before deciding.

The right choice is context-dependent: tail-based is worth the extra complexity when budget is tight and the team mainly needs to catch rare errors/slowdowns, while simple head-based is still acceptable for a small system or one lacking the operational resources to run a stateful collector.
Root bug #1: `span.end()` is only reached on the success path — when `charge_gateway(order_id)` throws, execution jumps out of the function before `span.set_attribute` and `span.end()` ever run.

Consequence of bug #1: depending on the SDK's behavior, the span is either fully lost (never reaches the collector, matching the "some timed-out requests leave no span at all" symptom) or, if the SDK garbage-collects orphaned spans, its recorded duration is inaccurate.
Root bug #2 (independent of bug #1): the code never calls `span.record_exception(e)` or `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR))` on any path.

Consequence of bug #2: successful and failed spans end up with identical fields/status, so they can't be told apart in Tempo's waterfall view — matching the "failed traces look identical to successful ones" symptom.

Fix for bug #1: wrap the call in try/except/finally, or better, use the context manager `with tracer.start_as_current_span("process_payment") as span:` so `end()` is called automatically whether or not an exception occurred.
Fix for bug #2: in the except branch, call `span.record_exception(e)` and `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, description=str(e)))` before re-raising the exception, without swallowing it.

Verify: mock `charge_gateway` to throw, call `process_payment`, and confirm the span still appears (not lost), carries `status=ERROR` with an attached exception event, clearly distinguishable from a successful trace of the same function.

Uses the context manager `with tracer.start_as_current_span("apply_discount") as span:` instead of manual `start_span()`/`end()`, guaranteeing `span.end()` is always called automatically even if an exception is thrown from any line inside the block.

Calls `span.set_attribute` for `cart_id` and `coupon_code` right at the top of the block, before any logic that could fail, so the attributes always appear on the span regardless of later errors (setting attributes at the end of a function is a common mistake since a mid-function error would prevent that line from ever running).

Handles the invalid-coupon case with `span.add_event("invalid_coupon", {cart_id, coupon_code})` because it's a noteworthy milestone in normal processing flow (not a system error) — does not use `record_exception`/`set_status(ERROR)` for this case.

When `charge_discount_engine` genuinely throws an exception (a technical error), wraps the call in `try/except` and calls `span.record_exception(e)` to record the exception as an event on the span, capturing its stack trace.

Separately calls `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(e)))` to mark the whole span itself as errored — a distinct signal from recording the exception, since a span can log an exception event without its overall status being ERROR.
Re-raises the exception after recording it (does not swallow it) so the caller's error-handling logic still works normally, since tracing only observes and doesn't change business behavior.
Core constraint: the tail-sampling processor must see ALL of a trace's spans (across all services) before it can decide whether to keep or drop that trace.

In contrast, head-based sampling decisions are made independently per service — no service needs to know about another service's spans on the same trace — so head-based collector instances can run completely independently and be load-balanced randomly/round-robin with no problem.

With tail-based sampling, if spans of the same trace_id get scattered randomly across independent collector instances, no single instance sees enough of the whole trace to decide correctly — meaning a tail-sampling collector cannot simply be scaled horizontally like an ordinary stateless service.

The correct architecture is two-tiered: a lightweight 'agent' collector runs alongside each service (sidecar or DaemonSet) whose only job is to receive spans and forward them, making no sampling decision itself.
The second tier is a centralized 'gateway' collector cluster that actually runs the tail_sampling processor.

Agents must forward to the gateway using load balancing BY trace_id (e.g. a loadbalancing exporter that hashes trace_id), not random round-robin, so every span of the same trace_id — regardless of which agent it came from — routes to exactly one gateway instance where the whole trace can accumulate before a decision is made.

The biggest trade-off is memory: the gateway must hold all of a trace's spans in RAM until the trace is considered complete (via a decision_wait timeout, e.g. 10-30 seconds), which at tens of thousands of requests/second from 50 services requires significant RAM and upfront capacity planning — not a 'flip a flag and it just works' config.

Rollout should be gradual: enable tail-sampling for a portion of traffic or a subset of services first, monitor the gateway cluster's RAM/CPU (to catch OOM risk during spikes) and the rate of traces forced into a late decision due to decision_wait timeout (a sign of overload or too-short timeout), then expand gradually to the whole system.

Root cause: over-instrumentation — creating a separate span for EVERY processing step, including tiny, synchronous ones that are never meaningfully slow or error-prone (e.g. validating a field, a simple multiplication/addition).

Cost consequence: every span carries its own overhead (creating the object, serializing, exporting over the network to the collector), so 22 spans for a simple request means 8x the volume of a reasonable instrumentation, exploding storage/network cost.

Readability consequence: the Tempo waterfall becomes too long to read because dozens of no-diagnostic-value micro-spans (validate_field_customer_id, compute_subtotal, ...) inflate its length with steps that are always fast and almost never fail.

That clutter specifically drowns out the two spans that actually matter — call_inventory_service and call_payment_service — exactly where real network I/O can be slow or fail, which is what an on-call needs to see immediately upon opening the trace.

Correct principle: only create a separate span at points with real diagnostic value — service boundaries (network calls), I/O (DB queries, cache), or genuinely complex/error-prone logic — while all synchronous internal validate/compute steps are merged into a single parent span (not dropping tracking, just not needing a separate span per sub-step).

Rewrite: refactor process_order into 4 spans instead of 22 — validate_order and compute_total each wrap their internal synchronous sub-steps in one block, while call_inventory_service and call_payment_service each keep their own dedicated span since that's where real errors/slowness can genuinely occur.
Verify quantitatively: measure span count per request before/after confirming the drop from 22 to 4, and confirm the system's overall span volume drops proportionally to the per-request reduction.
Verify qualitatively: open the Tempo waterfall confirming it's readable in a few seconds and immediately shows the two service calls as the most time-consuming/important spans.
Chỉ ra t3 thuộc burstable family với cơ chế CPU credit: baseline chỉ 5-40% tuỳ size, tích credit khi chạy dưới baseline và tiêu credit khi chạy trên baseline.

Giải thích t family được thiết kế cho workload KHÔNG ĐỀU (dev/test, traffic web dao động), không phù hợp cho workload CPU-bound chạy liên tục 24/7 như video encoding — nên chọn t3.large cho job này là sai ngay từ đầu.
Nêu đúng cơ chế gây chậm: job chạy trên baseline liên tục đốt CPUCreditBalance về 0 sau vài chục phút đến vài giờ (tuỳ size instance), sau đó AWS hard-throttle instance xuống đúng baseline.
Giải thích vì sao CloudWatch CPU utilization trông 'không hẳn 100%' khi bị throttle, khiến dễ nhầm là do code chậm trong khi thực chất là do hạ tầng ghìm lại ở mức baseline.
Nêu cách xác nhận nguyên nhân thật: theo dõi CPUCreditBalance trên CloudWatch, nếu giảm về 0 đúng lúc job chậm thì đó là bằng chứng trực tiếp của credit throttling.

Đưa ra hướng khắc phục đúng: chuyển sang c family (compute optimized, vCPU:RAM = 1:2), không có cơ chế credit nên không bao giờ bị throttle dù chạy full CPU liên tục, phù hợp với CPU-bound batch job như video encoding.

Đề cập giải pháp tạm thời credit_specification.cpu_credits = "unlimited" để trả phụ phí thay vì bị throttle khi chưa đổi family ngay được, nhưng nhấn mạnh đây chỉ là stopgap tốn thêm chi phí, không phải hướng đúng lâu dài cho workload CPU-bound liên tục.
